blocks.x: Why shared spaces matter more now

Winnipeg tenants may have more choices, which makes apartment lobby renovation ideas worth a closer look. By October 2026, [liv.rent's report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) showed unfurnished one-bedroom asking rents down three months in a row, and the [City of Winnipeg](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-08-20-winnipeg-leads-major-canadian-cities-housing-growth) reported housing completions up 52.7% in the first seven months of the year.

In offices, [CBRE's January 2026 outlook](https://www.cbre.com/insights/articles/whats-ahead-for-winnipeg-commercial-real-estate-in-2026) describes a flight to quality, with tenants moving up to Class A buildings. New buildings often set the standard with attractive lobbies, lounges, package rooms and well-lit corridors. Older buildings have to compete.
The hospitality mindset
Hotels design for experience. Every surface a guest sees and touches is chosen to create an impression and stand up to heavy use. Key principles:
**The arrival moment matters most.** The entrance and lobby set expectations.
**Consistency builds trust.** Hallways, elevators and doors should look cared for throughout.
**Durability is design.** Finishes must look good after years of use.
**Lighting changes everything.** Good lighting makes spaces feel safe and welcoming.
**Details signal care.** Clean doors, consistent hardware and fresh paint show attention.

blocks.x: Our view: shared spaces are a high-value upgrade

For a building owner, upgrading shared spaces has a major advantage over unit work: every tenant benefits. A refreshed lobby and corridors can improve how every resident or office tenant feels about the building, and every prospective tenant sees them on a tour.
Shared-space projects can also be easier to schedule. They can often be done without entering units, and work can be phased floor by floor.
Finish choices that last
Hotels choose finishes for durability, and property managers should too:
**Flooring:** commercial-grade LVP or carpet tile handles heavy traffic and is easy to replace in sections.
**Paint:** scrubbable, high-durability finishes in corridors and lobbies.
**Doors:** solid-core suite doors can reduce noise and look better over time, but suite doors are often part of the fire separation, so check requirements before replacing them.
**Wall protection:** corner guards and durable wall surfaces in high-traffic areas.
Learning from the hospitality sector

Hotels often renovate in phases, by room, floor or wing, so the rest of the property keeps operating. Property managers can use the same approach: plan a refresh cycle for shared spaces every several years, rather than waiting until they look worn.
Questions to ask before starting

Before remodelling shared spaces, property managers should ask: What do prospective tenants notice on tours? What do current tenants complain about? Which areas show the most wear? What do competing buildings offer? And what budget is available this year and over the next several years?
The answers will point to where a refresh will have the most impact.

Then check the rules. The City's [commercial alteration guide](https://legacy.winnipeg.ca/ppd/Documents/Permits/CommercialAlterationDesignSummary/Guide-Commercial-Alteration-Design-Summary.pdf) says cosmetic work such as flooring and painting needs no building permit, though minor electrical, plumbing or ventilation work needs a trade permit. In larger buildings (Part 3 of the building code), significant changes to exits, lobbies used as exits, public corridors or fire separations need an architect or engineer.
In an older building, [test old flooring and adhesive for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before it comes up.
A phased refresh plan

A practical approach for many buildings is a three-stage refresh. First, the entrance and lobby, because they affect every visit and tour. Second, the corridors, floor by floor, with [durable flooring](/services/flooring), fresh paint and consistent suite doors. Third, amenity spaces such as a lounge, package room or shared work area, if the building has room.

Each stage delivers a visible improvement, and the work can be spread across one or more budget years. Starting with the entrance also gives leasing staff something new to show on tours, while later stages are planned and priced.
The bottom line

Shared spaces shape how people feel about a building. By borrowing the hospitality approach, focusing on arrival, consistency, durability and detail, property managers can make older buildings more competitive without renovating every unit. Small, consistent improvements, renewed on a regular cycle, can do more for a building's reputation than one large renovation followed by years of neglect.
